summary: loop.run_in_executor(None, ...) all share one bounded default ThreadPoolExecutor; saturating it with blocking calls makes every other default-executor call queue and stall. Give bulk blocking work its own executor.
symptoms: run_in_executor calls hang or stall under load
unrelated async task blocked waiting for a free thread pool worker
quick executor call takes seconds when many blocking calls are running
asyncio app latency spikes when offloading many blocking functions to the default executor

preconditions: Multiple loop.run_in_executor(None, ...) calls offloading blocking work
Number of concurrent blocking calls >= the default pool's max_workers
Blocking calls hold their worker for a non-trivial duration

problem: loop.run_in_executor(None, func) uses the event loop's single shared default ThreadPoolExecutor, whose max_workers is bounded (min(32, cpu_count+4) by default). When that many blocking calls are in flight, every additional run_in_executor(None, ...) call — including unrelated ones elsewhere in the app — queues behind them and stalls until a worker frees up. Because the pool is shared and its size is small, one blocking workload silently starves the latency of everything else offloaded to the default executor. The size varies by machine, so the bug can hide in dev and surface under production concurrency.
procedure: Create a dedicated ThreadPoolExecutor for the bulk/blocking workload and pass it explicitly: `loop.run_in_executor(bulk_ex, func, ...)`, leaving the default executor free for latency-sensitive calls.
Size the dedicated pool for its workload; use `with ThreadPoolExecutor(...) as ex:` so it is shut down deterministically.
For CPU-bound work, use a ProcessPoolExecutor instead — threads cannot parallelize CPU work under the GIL and will still starve the pool.
If you must share the default pool, cap concurrency yourself (e.g. an asyncio.Semaphore) so it never fully saturates.
anti_patterns: Assuming run_in_executor(None, ...) gives unbounded parallelism — it is capped by one small shared pool.
Offloading many long blocking calls to the default executor alongside latency-sensitive ones — the latter starve.
Using threads (any executor) for CPU-bound work and expecting speedup — the GIL serializes it and the pool stays saturated.

failed_attempts.approach: Offloading all blocking work to the default executor via run_in_executor(None, ...) and expecting each call to run promptly
failed_attempts.why_it_fails: The default pool has only min(32, cpu+4) workers; once saturated, further calls queue. Latency-sensitive calls sharing the default pool stall behind the bulk work with no error raised.

files.test_fix.py:
import asyncio
import time
import sys
import concurrent.futures

def blocking(secs):
    time.sleep(secs)

async def main():
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    probe = concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(); size = probe._max_workers; probe.shutdown()

    # FIX: bulk blocking work gets its OWN executor; default stays free
    with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=size) as bulk_ex:
        long_tasks = [loop.run_in_executor(bulk_ex, blocking, 0.5) for _ in range(size)]
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)  # let the bulk pool fill

        t0 = time.monotonic()
        await loop.run_in_executor(None, blocking, 0.01)  # default pool, uncontended
        quick_latency = time.monotonic() - t0

        await asyncio.gather(*long_tasks)

    assert quick_latency < 0.3, f'quick call was starved: {quick_latency:.3f}s'
    print(f'SUCCESS: quick call stayed responsive ({quick_latency:.3f}s) with a dedicated executor')

asyncio.run(main())
sys.exit(0)
